To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the power spectral density of a first-order discrete-time Markov model is given by the formula P(f) = 2(1 - p) (p + (1 - p) e-i2πf)/[(1 - p)2 + 2(1-p) cos(2πf) + 1] and that this formula can be used to estimate the non-zero state value, the number of identical chains and the non-unity transition probability of the model.
the power spectrum of an individual channel recording is a function of the non-zero state probability, the noise variance, and the eigenvalues of the transition matrix.

(i) the mean, variance and third central moment are sufficient statistics for the estimation of parameters of a first-order Markov chain; and (ii) the power spectrum of an independent, binary, first-order Markov signal in white noise is sufficient for the estimation of its non-unity eigenvalues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of individual channel kinetics in recordings containing many identical, independent, identical, independent, non-homogeneous channels observed in white noise.
the estimation of the elementary parameters of a Markov process given a noisy signal containing many independent, identical copies of that process.
the estimation of the number of independent Markov chains, the non-zero state value, and the elementary transition matrix from a noisy signal consisting of many independent Markov chains.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our results show that it is possible to estimate the parameters of a first-order Markov chain from a noisy signal consisting of many independent, identical chains, provided that the noise level is not too high and the transition matrix is not very close to the identity matrix.
the power spectrum provides sufficient information to identify the individual kinetics of the channels.
we have developed a method for identifying individual channel kinetics from noisy recordings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have provided a theoretical and numerical basis for the identification of the kinetics of a single ion channel, given a signal containing many identical, independent channels.
we have shown that the power spectrum of an observed signal can provide sufficient information for estimation of the parameters that describe the signal.

the mean and variance of the noisy signal provide sufficient information for estimating the parameters of the underlying signal, and the power spectrum can provide additional information for the estimation procedure, especially when the signal-to-noise ratio is low.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to estimate the number of independent channels, the non-unity transition matrix, and the noise variance of the signal using a simple, non-iterative, linear estimation procedure.
, in the case of noisy signals, the power spectrum of such a signal is a useful diagnostic tool for the identification of the parameters of interest.
the estimation of the transition probability matrix from a noisy signal is a tractable problem that is amenable to a variety of methods.
